st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source does not directly assess whether cheaper legal assistance can expand access to justice while preserving consumer protection and accountability. It instead shifts the focus to transformation of legal practice and the continuing need for lawyers in social value judgments, while using an unchecked-citation episode to distinguish hallucinated authorities from potentially valid arguments.
qs: Until then, lawyers will be called upon to help make social value judgments.

st.t: Legal prediction: Classification cannot guarantee sound advice
st.an: The source shifts the issue from whether classification can guarantee sound legal advice to whether routine, settled-law tasks are predictable enough for cost-driven automation and lawyer substitution. Its distinction between straightforward cases and disputes involving complicated factual records leaves the cluster’s limits on prediction and advice unresolved rather than rejecting them.
qs: Large and consistent datasets engender easy predictability and automation.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source does not substantively address buyer-led workflow unbundling or challenges to time-based pricing. Instead, it shifts the analysis to supply-side economics: proprietary-model investment may encourage law-firm consolidation and strengthen firm-level client attachment, while increasingly capable models reduce reliance on lawyers for routine work. These predictions complement parts of the cluster but materially reframe its central proposition.
qs: But there is a related and perhaps more important question; that is, whether the economics of LLMs will encourage a wave of consolidation within the legal services market.

In the longer term, large language models threaten to weaken the attorneys‟ monopoly on analytical skill tout court, especially when that skill is called upon to complete a routine legal task that the model has seen many times before.

st.t: AI infrastructure: Scale advantages need not create monopoly
st.an: The source accepts that compute and capital create meaningful scale advantages, but argues these need not harden into monopoly because legal-data exclusivity may weaken, low-cost models may catch up, and hardware and model-efficiency improvements may reduce barriers. It materially develops the cluster through a detailed make-or-buy account in which specialist suppliers gain scale economies while recurring processing costs remain significant.
qs: One can conclude in sum, albeit somewhat tentatively, that competitive advantage based upon unique access to excellent data will wane as LLMs continue their ascent.

PROCESSING POWER AND FIRM ORGANIZATION      Even if legal data is difficult to hoard, competitive advantage will be acquired, and for a while maintained, through access to processing power made possible through capital investment.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The source accepts that fabricated citations require verification while materially developing the cluster’s distinction between citation authenticity and argument quality. Its compression analogy explains how a legal argument may remain defensible despite false authorities, without treating fabricated citations as acceptable or establishing any general error-rate trajectory.
qs: It is curious that the citations were manifestly fake, while their surrounding text and arguments were simultaneously correct and defensible.
In law, compression is a virtue, not a form of deceit or an act of fraud.10 Lawyers distill rules from patterns observed in cases and other contexts and leverage the familiar.

st.t: Litigation responsibility: Sanctions follow conduct and authority
st.an: The source accepts continuing lawyer responsibility for citation verification and reinforces the cluster’s distinction between argument quality and citation integrity with benchmark evidence. Its Mata discussion also materially develops the point that concealment and misleading responses after discovery can elevate culpability beyond the initial failure.
qs: Guha et al., supra note 41 (documenting benchmark tests in which ChatGPT-4 reaches correct legal conclusions and provides correct legal reasoning 82.2 and 79.7 percent of time while simultaneously identifying correct citations just 59.2 percent of the time).

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The source accepts that technical accuracy cannot itself legitimate autonomous adjudication and materially develops the proposition by explaining that lawmaking and precedent change require human choices about social goals and values. It therefore argues for continued human control, with AI assisting lawyers rather than independently determining law.
qs: Even a fully matured AI that makes few mistakes may pursue goals contrary to human preferences and values if given full autonomy to set social policies and create law.248 By maintaining control of lawmaking, society ensures that its rules are aligned with its preferences.
When societal and technological innovation provoke reversals of prior precedent, or stimulate questions of first impression, social goals and preferences must be calibrated or set anew.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s premise that AI can automate scalable associate work and reduce associate staffing, although it does not address the resulting verification paradox or proposals for reconstructing apprenticeship.
qs: The role of the associate is severely diminished.

In-house proprietary language models used for practice areas where law is settled and where legal services can scale will place downward pressure on the need for numerous associates and partners alike.98      On the other hand, it is more difficult to keep the data related to scaled legal practice private.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The source directly accepts the cluster’s principal proposition: LegalBench offers only a rough, incomplete estimate of task-specific capability, and current non-specialized models remain far from a practicable substitute for lawyers. Its forecast that mature specialized systems may automate routine work is explicitly conditional and does not convert present benchmark scores into evidence of dependable autonomous lawyering.
qs: First, diagnostic testing of non-specialized foundation models reveals growth in accuracy, but levels still fall well short of indicating a practicable alternative to lawyers.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that lawyers remain accountable for AI-assisted filings, human supervision is necessary, and sanctions principally address failed inquiry or deceptive conduct rather than AI use itself. It is more optimistic than the cluster about model reliability and the sufficiency of sanctions alone, but those qualifications do not displace its overall endorsement of supervised use and human verification.
qs: At least one judge has posted a standing order that any attorney or pro se litigant appearing before his court must file a certificate attesting that language models will not be used to draft a portion of any filing, or if a language model is used, then the model‟s output must checked for accuracy by a human being using traditional legal databases or print reporters.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source accepts that lawyers should remain actively involved in supervising AI output and exercising independent judgment, especially by deciding when to defer to or override the system. This aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on meaningful human control, although the source does not develop the cluster’s concerns about verification, expertise development, or the adequacy of professional rules, and its claimed team advantage rests on analogy rather than legal-performance evidence.
qs: There is a strong case to be made, therefore, that a substantial portion of a future attorney‟s effort and work will take the form of continual interaction with the firm‟s language model and supervision of its output.
However, on occasion, he overrules the machine when he sees what he believes is a potentially better move.

It does not establish that mitigation can eliminate verification; the reported prediction that hallucinations will disappear is attributed to Altman rather than adopted or evidenced.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Fagan supports the cluster’s core account: current models are not practical lawyer replacements, routine work is increasingly automatable, and lawyers retain supervision, non-routine judgment and empathy. He also calls for recalibrating legal education and training. His stronger, conditional prediction of substantial long-run headcount reduction is more aggressive than the synthesis, but does not displace his near-term emphasis on supervised task reconfiguration.
qs: In a world of advanced language models, machines will carry out much of the lawyer‟s routine work, but non-routine tasks will continue to benefit from human analytical and empathetic input.170 Before discussing these two       167           This is because the LLM will find it comparatively more difficult to produce attorney work product from few relevant examples.
It necessitates a reevaluation of the lawyer‟s role, the recalibration of legal education and training, and a thoughtful approach to the ethical and practical implications of AI in law.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that AI entails professional and organisational transformation rather than simple task automation, while preserving human judgment in complex legal work. It also aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on data and processing capabilities as sources of competitive advantage. Its contribution is narrower and predictive, offering little evidence on bargaining shifts among legal departments, ALSPs and AI-native providers, realised returns or pricing change.
qs: The intersection of AI and human expertise will likely define the new frontier of legal practice, where lawyers leverage AI for efficiency while contributing their irreplaceable human judgment and empathetic understanding in shaping and applying the law.
Moreover, the evolving landscape suggests that data quality and processing capabilities will become crucial competitive edges.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that model access alone is unlikely to create durable competitive advantage. It predicts broadly comparable third-party AI capabilities and questions whether bespoke in-house models justify heavy investment, reinforcing the importance of effective processing and delivery rather than technology ownership itself. Its claims are forecasts, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: And firms therefore will be able to process data with comparable skill and effectiveness, and at comparable cost.
However, it is not immediately apparent whether one firm can outperform another by investing heavily in the construction and maintenance of an in-house, customized model.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s near-term framing of legal AI as an unreliable substitute for lawyers, citing capability and accuracy limitations in routine legal work. It does not directly assess whether verification consumes efficiency gains or detail lifecycle confidentiality controls, and its possibility of long-term lawyer displacement is a forecast rather than a rejection of present human oversight.
qs: For a time, models will be weak substitutes for lawyers for the completion of standard legal tasks.
will address generative A.I.‟s current state of the art in law, and especially, its limitations in accuracy with respect to routine legal tasks.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition by arguing that language models directly automate core legal tasks, particularly research and writing, while treating substantial automation as a forecast rather than established job displacement. Its acknowledgment of past failed displacement predictions and the technology’s maturation period aligns with the cluster’s caution about aggregate staffing outcomes.
qs: Large language models, as automated research and writing tools, take aim directly at the core activities of legal practice.
will automate 44% of legal tasks within ten years of widespread adoption.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that AI-driven legal delivery will combine technology with human expertise and reshape competition through organisational capabilities rather than simple task automation. It specifically predicts that data and processing capabilities will confer competitive advantage and may promote consolidation, while treating these outcomes as forecasts rather than established findings.
qs: The intersection of AI and human expertise will likely define the new frontier of legal practice, where lawyers leverage AI for efficiency while contributing their irreplaceable human judgment and empathetic understanding in shaping and applying the law.

Law firms that can harness superior data and more efficient processing will likely lead the field, potentially ushering in greater market consolidation and a redefinition of what constitutes a leading law firm in the digital age.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the application-layer thesis by presenting Harvey as specialised legal AI used beyond research, particularly for contract review. It also aligns with the synthesis’s evidentiary caution: broader work-product uses and firm-specific security restrictions are treated as inferences, while security protections are reported largely through vendor assurances. It does not establish commercial defensibility or durable leadership.
qs: For instance, Harvey carries out contract review and has achieved an error rate lower than that of an average attorney.94 Allen & Overy has not disclosed precisely how its attorneys use the Harvey-made LLM, but it is easy to imagine that it has been used to develop attorney work product beyond contracts, given that the lawyers asked the bot questions across 250 practice areas.
Harvey‟s “trust report” touts a number of guarantees of compliance, including with the California Consumer Protection Act, as well as 37 controls spanning 5 categories.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, task-sensitive deployment: it treats current models as inadequate substitutes for lawyers, preserves human roles in supervision, novel disputes and value judgments, and calls for redesigning professional roles and training. It goes further than the cluster by predicting eventual substitution of much routine work, but presents that outcome as conditional and not imminent.
qs: First, diagnostic testing of non-specialized foundation models reveals growth in accuracy, but levels still fall well short of indicating a practicable alternative to lawyers.
It necessitates a reevaluation of the lawyer‟s role, the recalibration of legal education and training, and a thoughtful approach to the ethical and practical implications of AI in law.

kp.k: Near-term expansion precedes predicted long-term lawyer displacement
kp.d: Fagan predicts that LLMs will initially generate legal work concerning data ownership, generated output, prompts, torts and risk management. Once the technology matures and governing rules settle, he anticipates substitution for routine research and drafting, fewer lawyers and potentially greater consolidation. These are conditional forecasts rather than observed employment findings, and the paper does not specify when mature substitution will occur.
qs: In the near term, LLMs will spur new legal work.
Consequently, legal tasks will take less time to complete, and language models will enhance lawyer productivity.
Even if the end of lawyers or their severe reduction may be on the horizon, a change is not imminent.

kp.k: Data advantages depend on quality, exclusivity and scale
kp.d: The paper distinguishes web-level, industry-level and firm-level data. Fagan argues that specialized legal data can improve output, but doubts that private data necessarily creates durable advantages: sufficiently numerous examples and effective modeling may erase small quality differences, while public filings, lawyer mobility and expanding client bases spread know-how. Confidential transactional documents may remain exclusive longer than litigation work product.
qs: The following sections thus describe a hierarchy of data across three levels: the web, industry, and firm.
It is difficult to keep relatively identical services private.
One can conclude in sum, albeit somewhat tentatively, that competitive advantage based upon unique access to excellent data will wane as LLMs continue their ascent.

kp.k: Specialized models combine generation with legal databases
kp.d: Fagan describes layered systems combining foundation models, legal training or fine-tuning, database searches and citation-checking tools, identifying LexisNexis and Harvey as examples of this anticipated deployment pattern. He expects specialized models to outperform general-purpose models in the short to medium term, while leaving open whether inexpensive or open-source alternatives will ultimately match proprietary capabilities.
qs: The point is that there are many creative ways to add a specialized layer focused on law and legal tasks that can interact with a foundation language model to output excellent results.
While it is conceivable that general-purpose and specialized LLMs could eventually achieve identical capabilities, it is unclear how long such an achievement would take.

kp.k: Affordable models could narrow competitive gaps
kp.d: If excellent commercial models remain affordable, Fagan expects widespread adoption and productivity gains for solo practitioners and smaller firms, partially narrowing their disadvantage against larger firms. Competition would shift away from processing public information toward exclusive information and computational investment. He separately notes potential benefits for occasional non-lawyer users from high-quality open-source models; these possibilities are not measured access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: If most lawyers are using excellent LLMs, productivity in legal services should increase across the board.
To the extent that they can wield this tool effectively, they should be expected to at least partially close the competitive gap between themselves and larger firms.
On the other hand, non-lawyers who would like to use a commercial service only once or twice will greatly benefit from high-quality, open-source language models.

kp.k: Confidentiality creates demand for trusted model providers
kp.d: Fagan identifies potential disclosure of client facts, litigation strategy and negotiated terms through model use. He discusses collection opt-outs and enterprise security arrangements, but emphasizes dependence on provider trust and legal remedies for breaches. His account predicts purchases from established legal information providers or specialized vendors offering convincing security, rather than reporting that such arrangements eliminate confidentiality risks.
qs: Even if the data is stripped of identifying information, a language model may still be able to identify patterns or practices, especially if a lawyer or firm uses the model often enough.
Additional security can also be purchased.

kp.k: Harvey pilot demonstrates reported adoption, not proven displacement
kp.d: Citing Allen & Overy and contemporary reporting, Fagan describes a Harvey pilot beginning in November 2022: around 3,500 lawyers asked some 40,000 questions across 50 languages and 250 practice areas. The paper reports daily use in about 25% of practices and monthly use in 80%. It also repeats a reported contract-review error advantage over an average attorney without presenting an evaluation design or numerical error rate. Fagan's discussion of the firm's data-sharing and security terms is explicitly speculative.
qs: Those questions were asked in 50 languages across 250 practice areas.
About 25% of the firm‟s practices used the bot daily, and a remarkable 80% used the bot monthly.
While Harvey and Allen & Overy have not publicized the nature of their security arrangement

kp.k: Scalable routine work motivates investment and reduced staffing
kp.d: Fagan's hypothetical economics translate productivity improvements into possible labor savings rather than document actual reductions. The abstract suggests that a ten percent productivity increase could encourage an average-sized Big Law firm to cut 300 to 400 associates, saving $60 to $120 million. Separately, the body models 2,000 to 3,000 associates paid an average $300,000, implying $600 million to $900 million in associate labor costs and $60 million to $90 million savings at ten percent. He conditions investment on sufficient repeatable demand and identifies routine corporate legal department work as especially suitable.
qs: The role of the associate is severely diminished.

In-house proprietary language models used for practice areas where law is settled and where legal services can scale will place downward pressure on the need for numerous associates and partners alike.

Demand for lower-cost legal services based on language models will be especially strong in corporate legal departments that engage in routine transactions that often consist of distinct details relevant to the corporation‟s business.

kp.k: Boutique economics constrain automation and consolidation
kp.d: The paper argues that excellent data and powerful models are insufficient investment justifications where services do not scale. Its hypothetical small severance practice and nuclear regulatory practice illustrate situations where a few lawyers can already satisfy demand, leaving limited productivity benefits relative to model development and maintenance costs. Fagan treats these niches as a limit on broader consolidation predictions.
qs: In addition to access to data and processing power, scalability of services is a necessary ingredient.
The boutique‟s work does not scale.
It has already been emphasized that boutique services do not scale.

kp.d: Fagan generally expects near-term purchasing from third-party developers because model building and data management can be spread across multiple law-firm customers. His illustrative model costs $4 million to build; a vendor selling it to three firms for $1.5 million each earns $500,000 while undercutting separate construction. Proprietary development becomes more plausible with unique data, lower internal costs or consolidated scale, although the paper questions how often the first two conditions will hold.
qs: The likely path that firms will take in the near future will be to purchase generative A.I. services from a third-party vendor.
Perhaps the only good economic reason for developing a large language model in-house is scaled consolidation, that is, if X, Y, and Z were to merge.

kp.k: Processing costs create conditional scale advantages
kp.d: The paper predicts falling computing costs but argues that persistent costs combined with economies of scale could favor well-capitalized firms and mergers. It cites an estimated $12 million GPT-3 training cost and reports GPT-4 costs exceeding $60 million alongside rumored model-size figures. It also cites research covering 470 GPUs released between 2006 and 2021, finding performance per dollar doubled every 2.5 years, and treats future cost reductions as projections rather than established legal-market outcomes.
qs: Because GPUs are presently expensive, the cost of renting computational time on a cloud is high.
On the other hand, to the extent processing costs remain somewhat high and efficiently scale, LLMs could give way to a new wave of consolidation in the legal services market.

kp.k: Synthetic data promises savings but risks degradation
kp.d: Fagan proposes synthetic legal documents as a means to reduce preparation and processing costs, potentially with expert assessment guiding quality. He cites non-legal Amazon research as suggesting efficiency gains of as much as 22 percent, while acknowledging that the savings achievable with legal data are unknown. His illustrative mixture of 200 real and 300 synthetic documents reduces a $10 processing cost to $7 without quality loss by assumption, not measurement. He recognizes inaccurate assumptions, repeated synthetic training and changing conditions as risks.
qs: It is unclear to what extent processing costs can be reduced with synthetic legal data.
Synthetic data, of course, must adequately represent the real-world.
There is a fear that repeated use of synthetic data will lead to a decline in LLM capabilities over time.

kp.k: Firm-owned knowledge could weaken partner client portability
kp.d: Fagan hypothesizes that firm-controlled models could capture expertise through deliberate training and feedback, making clients less dependent on individual partners. If comparable analytical service remains available at the firm after a partner leaves, client retention and merger value become more predictable. He contrasts this scenario with today's fragmented, relationship-driven market, while acknowledging constraints from similar competing models, client preferences, non-scalable services and conflicts. Reduced reliance on lawyers is also presented as potentially easing internal separation of conflicting work.
qs: Large language models potentially shift the balance of power between attorneys and firms.
Specialized knowledge demanded by the client now rests with both the model and attorney, and the abilities of the model, as a centralized repository, quite possibly may exceed those of the attorney.
Inasmuch as lawyers and their clients become less tightly bound, the value of a law firm merger becomes more certain.

kp.k: Verification remains distinct from model performance
kp.d: The paper requires careful human review of contemporary general-purpose model output and separately discusses automated checking against legal authority. Fagan uses Mata v. Avianca to argue that fabricated citations need not imply wholly incorrect underlying legal propositions, and interprets its $5,000 sanctions as primarily addressing deception and persistence after warnings. His prediction that malpractice liability will remain near current levels rests on supervision, sanctions and existing competence standards; it is not an empirical finding about malpractice incidence.
qs: ChatGPT‟s work product must be carefully reviewed.
Supervision is a likely path for LLM usage in law in the short-term.

In sum, sanctions should be sufficient for suppressing generative errors ignored by casual supervision of LLM output; existing malpractice standards appear capable for answering legal questions of attorney competence as LLMs continue their ascent.

kp.k: Benchmarks support improvement, not autonomous practice readiness
kp.d: Fagan reports LegalBench results across 162 tasks and 20 foundation models, with GPT-4 performing best: issue spotting 82.9%, conclusion identification 89.9%, interpretation 75.2%, rhetoric 79.4% and citations 59.2%; rule application yielded correct results 82.2% and correct reasoning 79.7%. He separately reports Nay's fiduciary-obligation study improving from 27% for ChatGPT-3 to 78% for GPT-4. His extrapolation from a hypothetical 20% reasoning improvement to 95.7% accuracy is a forecast, not a demonstrated legal benchmark result.
qs: First, diagnostic testing of non-specialized foundation models reveals growth in accuracy, but levels still fall well short of indicating a practicable alternative to lawyers.
The model clearly struggled with identifying correct citations, reaching correct results just 59.2 percent of the time.
If so, then legal reasoning tasks would achieve an accuracy of 95.7 percent.

kp.k: AI creates transitional ownership, liability and transactional work
kp.d: Fagan identifies unresolved copyright questions concerning training data, compilations, synthetic output and engineered prompts, alongside hypothetical taxation and liability problems for ownerless AI. He predicts more precise risk assessment could support more detailed contracts, insurance, derivatives and asset partitioning. Additional tort questions concern developer precautions and unwanted actions by virtual assistants. These examples demonstrate possible sources of non-routine work, not recommendations for specific legal outcomes; the work becomes automatable as rules and practices settle.
qs: This Section does not predict or suggest how law and legal practice will evolve.
Legal questions surrounding property rights in data and the generated output of models will keep lawyers busy for a time.
As the novelty wanes and practices become settled, the transactional attorney‟s work product will become increasingly routinized and exposed to substitution by machines.

kp.k: Routine adjudication becomes a potential substitution domain
kp.d: Using Cardozo's historical account, Fagan distinguishes straightforward applications of settled law, uncertain factual applications of settled law, and decisions requiring new law. He predicts mature AI acting alone in the first category, often alone in the second, and alongside empathetic lawyers in the third. He supports the routine-work premise with Cardozo's observations and cited research reporting approximately 60% settlement in US federal courts and fewer than 5% of cases reaching trial after accounting for dismissals. These materials support his theoretical argument rather than directly measure AI substitutability.
qs: Part II has suggested that fully matured LLMs will complete most, if not all, routine legal tasks.
A language model can develop the ability to apply legal standards.

Under the assumption that language models will handle routine cases with minimal supervision and human oversight, the lawyer‟s role will be severely limited inasmuch as there are few non-routine legal tasks.

kp.k: Novelty, judgment and empathy preserve human roles
kp.d: Fagan predicts continuing demand for lawyers where sparse examples undermine prediction or disputes require choosing social goals, rights and resource allocations. He grounds the latter boundary in an assumption that humans retain political control, not solely in model accuracy. Lawyers would filter machine suggestions, advocate for affected parties and provide empathy. He also qualifies this comparative advantage: routine work requires less empathy, supervision skills may converge and preferences for personal contact may weaken; unusually sustained innovation could instead generate greater demand for non-routine legal work.
qs: When law presents novel scenarios with little data for analysis, human lawyers will likely remain significant actors.

Because humans have not (yet) conceded political decision-making to machines, it is likely that lawyers will be called upon to develop normative argument and represent parties, if only because they will be expected to empathize with those affected by social choices.
Of these four variables—supervision, empathy, model power, and model access—the attorney only controls the first two.
Until then, lawyers will be called upon to help make social value judgments.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Fagan predicts a transitional increase in new legal work, followed by automation of routine services, reduced demand for lawyers, and possible consolidation as expertise becomes embedded in firm-controlled models.
pts.d:
1. New legal work: Fagan predicts that LLMs initially generate demand for lawyers to resolve copyright and ownership questions concerning training data, outputs and prompts; address ownerless AI; refine transactional risk allocation; develop compliance practices; and determine tort liability. Better risk intelligence will support more detailed contracting and potentially greater use of insurance, derivatives and asset partitioning. As rules and practices settle, this work becomes increasingly susceptible to automation.

2. Routine-task substitution: Fagan predicts that mature LLMs will perform most or all routine research, writing and legal-standard application, eventually with minimal lawyer supervision. Initially they augment productivity; ultimately they substitute for substantial lawyer labor. He argues that routine work dominates legal practice, so continuing human roles in novel and value-laden matters will not necessarily preserve overall employment. His abstract states that a 10% productivity increase would encourage an average-sized Big Law firm to reduce associate headcount by 300–400, saving $60–$120 million. The body presents additional illustrative savings calculations rather than an observed employment effect.

3. Competitive differentiation: Fagan argues that legal-specialized models will generally outperform general-purpose models while their data and development confer superior capabilities. Widely affordable, excellent models could help solos and smaller firms narrow their competitive gap with large firms, reducing competition based on processing public legal information. Proprietary data and efficient computation become alternative sources of advantage. However, he tentatively predicts that data-based advantages will weaken as work product circulates, lawyers move between firms, and good models proliferate. Litigation work product is harder to keep proprietary than transactional documents.

4. Investment and scale: Fagan expects near-term reliance on third-party providers, but argues that substantial labor savings can justify proprietary model development, particularly when firms combine. Scalable, repetitive work under settled law provides the strongest investment case. Small specialist practices with limited client demand have less to gain from building in-house models. He predicts downward pressure on both associate and partner numbers in scalable practices, and strong demand for such systems in corporate legal departments.

5. Consolidation and partner power: Fagan predicts that models learning from lawyers can become firm-level repositories of expertise, reducing individual lawyers' exclusive possession of client-specific knowledge. Clients may consequently remain with firms rather than follow departing partners. More predictable client retention makes merger benefits more certain. Consolidation may arise either from expensive processing that rewards scale or from cheap, capable models that weaken lawyer-specific client ties. These are conditional hypotheses, not a forecast of a specified number of mergers.

6. Costs and adoption: Fagan expects hardware improvements, model specialization, compression, better querying and synthetic data to lower processing costs and encourage adoption. He also argues that residual computational costs could remain sufficiently high to reward scale. Synthetic legal data may reduce preparation and processing costs, provided it adequately represents the relevant real-world activity.

7. Verification and malpractice: Fagan predicts that supervision will characterize short-term legal use and that sanctions will encourage lawyers to check outputs. He argues that existing malpractice standards will generally remain adequate, that malpractice liability will probably remain near current levels, and that failure to use an LLM is unlikely by itself to establish malpractice. He distinguishes inaccurate citations and misleading conduct from the competence of the substantive legal work.

8. Residual human roles: Fagan predicts that lawyers will retain roles in genuinely novel matters, precedential change, normative advocacy, client relationships and output supervision. He argues that humans will continue to control social goals and value choices, and that lawyers' empathy will help them represent those affected by such choices. Nonetheless, he also suggests that differences in supervision and empathy skills may narrow, and demand for a personal touch may diminish, further weakening individual lawyers' bargaining power.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The paper combines economic hypotheticals, reported adoption figures, academic benchmarks, legal cases, historical judicial observations and cross-domain technical research; its employment and consolidation conclusions are principally conditional extrapolations.
pts.d:
1. Productivity and staffing: Fagan uses hypothetical lawyers and firms to calculate willingness to invest and potential salary savings. One example assumes a solo lawyer's $200,000 labor cost and a model performing 75% of her tasks; extending $150,000 in savings across 1,000 associates yields $150 million. He expressly calls this a toy example and notes that uniform linear savings across associates are probably unrealistic. A second calculation uses reported large-firm headcounts and associate salary ranges, assumes average associate pay of $300,000, and estimates savings of $6–$9 million at 1% productivity growth and $30–$45 million at 5%. These calculations support investment incentives, not measured layoffs or realized savings.

2. Adoption and performance reports: Fagan cites Allen & Overy's Harvey pilot, begun in November 2022, reporting approximately 3,500 lawyers asking 40,000 questions, across 50 languages and 250 practice areas; approximately 25% of practices reportedly used it daily and 80% monthly. He cites reporting that Harvey's contract-review error rate was below that of an average attorney, without supplying a test protocol or numerical error rate. His discussion of Allen & Overy's data-retention and security arrangements is explicitly conjectural. Harvey is the legal-AI company/product, not an individual lawyer.

3. LegalBench: Fagan draws on Guha and colleagues' academic benchmark covering 162 legal tasks and 20 foundation models. He reports GPT-4 accuracy of 82.9% for issue spotting, 89.9% for reaching conclusions, 75.2% for interpretation, 79.4% for rhetoric, and 59.2% for citation identification. For rule application, he separately reports 82.2% correct results and 79.7% correct reasoning, compared with GPT-3.5's 58.5% and 44.2%. He describes these diagnostics as an incomplete, rough estimate of capability, not evidence that models can replace lawyers in practice.

4. Legal-standard application and projected improvement: Fagan cites John Nay's fiduciary-duty study as reporting improvement from 27% correct identification with GPT-3 to 78% with GPT-4. He extrapolates toward judge-level application of standards. He also cites chain-of-thought prompting research for gains as high as 40%, then hypothesizes that a 20% relative improvement on 79.7% legal reasoning accuracy would yield 95.7%. That last figure is a scenario, not an observed legal benchmark result.

5. Author experience: Fagan reproduces his GPT-4 exchanges about a university's race-conscious admissions algorithm, describing basic doctrinal competence but failure to incorporate the effect of Students for Fair Admissions even after prompting. He also provides a removal-notice example and discloses that GPT-4 drafted the conclusion, which he revised lightly after asking for a less bombastic style. These are illustrative experiences rather than systematic evaluations.

6. Economic structure: The consolidation argument relies on transaction-cost and scale reasoning, hypotheticals about model ownership and client portability, and commentary on legal-market fragmentation. It does not supply observed AI-driven merger outcomes. Likewise, the proposition that proprietary legal data advantages will erode is supported through reasoning about public filings, diffusion of know-how, lawyer mobility and hypothetical synthetic-data training.

7. Cost trends: Fagan cites estimated GPT-3 training costs of $12 million and reported or rumored GPT-4 training and architecture figures, including costs above $60 million. He cites GPU price-performance research using 470 models released in 2006–2021, reporting a doubling of processing power per dollar every 2.5 years, alongside hardware and model-compression research. These are technical and cross-domain inputs to the legal-market projections.

8. Synthetic data: Fagan cites synthetic-data scholarship, Amazon research involving Alexa tasks, and research on degradation from recursive model-generated training data. He describes the Amazon result as an efficiency gain of approximately 22.6%, but states that the extent of savings for synthetic legal data remains unclear. His example reducing query costs from $10 to $7 with a real/synthetic document mix is hypothetical.

9. Malpractice and future work: Fagan discusses Mata v. Avianca, its $5,000 sanctions and the court's treatment of misleading conduct, together with Judge Brantley Starr's human-checking certification requirement. These are sanctions and verification examples, not measured hallucination or malpractice rates. Copyright litigation, Thaler v. Perlmutter, existing professional-care standards and tort scholarship support his discussion of new legal questions.

10. Rarity of non-routine work: Fagan relies on Cardozo's historical account of a docket dominated by settled-law application, and Chang and Klerman's reported approximately 60% federal settlement rate and less than 5% trial rate after accounting for dismissal. He uses these materials to support the proposition that precedent-changing work is relatively rare. His empathy and human-control predictions primarily rest on normative and institutional reasoning, with cross-domain human–AI chess examples offered for the possible value of combined human-machine work.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Fagan distinguishes a near-term period of limited capability, supervision and new legal demand from a longer-term scenario of mature models and settled rules; he offers no firm date for large-scale lawyer displacement.
pts.d:
The source is a working paper dated 22 March 2024, with a title page identifying Tennessee Law Review publication as forthcoming in 2025. Its statements about current tools are situated in that period.

Near term: Fagan expects firms to buy broadly available third-party services, lawyers to check output, and new AI-related legal issues to generate work. He describes general-purpose model output as comparable to a law student or perhaps first-year associate and says foundation-model diagnostic accuracy remains short of a practicable substitute for lawyers.

Short to medium term: Specialized legal models are expected to retain an advantage over general-purpose systems. Rules on property, liability, compliance and contracting must develop. High data and processing costs may encourage combinations that spread investment costs, but vendor comparative advantage can favor outsourcing instead of in-house development.

Long term: Substantial substitution depends on mature models producing reliable work, settled legal rules, sufficient relevant data, economically scalable demand and reduced need for human oversight. Routine legal standards are included in potential automation; genuinely novel facts, changing contexts and unsettled normative choices remain limits. Firm-controlled learning and client dependence on the resulting expertise underpin the client-retention mechanism. More equal model access, superior individual supervision or stronger client demand for empathy can limit the loss of lawyer-specific advantage.

Cost and competition qualifications: If high-quality data and processing are cheap and widely available, Fagan allows for excellent services, smaller quality differences and meaningful price competition instead of strong technology-based concentration. Boutique services that do not scale constrain consolidation. Synthetic data must adequately reflect reality; otherwise errors or degradation can outweigh savings. Continued technological and social innovation can create fresh non-routine work, and Fagan explicitly allows that a hyper-innovative society could sustain strong lawyer demand.

Specific horizons are mostly attributed external forecasts or illustrative extrapolations. Fagan cites Goldman Sachs as predicting automation of 44% of legal tasks within ten years of widespread adoption, while noting criticism of that forecast. He cites an external synthetic-data forecast extending to 2030. His own hardware scenario suggests that a continuation of past cost trends could halve a $60 million training cost twice before the end of the decade, while even one halving would be substantial. These are not firm dates for legal-sector transformation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects differ by scale, work type, ownership of models and client relationships: large scalable practices face staffing and organizational change, while specialists and value-oriented advocates retain differentiated roles.
pts.d:
Associates and junior lawyers: Routine research, drafting and document work are most directly exposed to substitution. Fagan predicts a severely diminished associate role in scalable practices, while describing present general-purpose output as requiring the scrutiny given to junior work.

Partners and rainmakers: Model-enabled capacity may reduce partner requirements as well as associate requirements. Firm-owned repositories can capture expertise formerly held by individuals, reducing client portability and bargaining power. Supervision, client interaction, strategy and empathy remain potential differentiators, although Fagan expects models to absorb some patterns from pre-writing activities too.

Large law firms: Large repeat workloads make substantial investment potentially worthwhile. Firms may compete on computational efficiency and proprietary model capabilities, consolidate to achieve scale, and retain clients more securely after partner departures or mergers.

Solo practitioners and smaller firms: Affordable commercial or open-source models may increase speed and accuracy and partly narrow competitive disadvantages. Conversely, unequal access to useful data or processing can preserve disadvantages. Fagan distinguishes inexpensive access to third-party tools from the usually weaker economic case for building a model to serve only a small practice.

Boutiques and specialists: Low-volume, highly specialized practices offer less scope for scaling model investment. Stable, repetitive and sufficiently numerous matters create stronger automation incentives than work involving unusual facts or continuously changing law.

Corporate legal departments and general counsel: Fagan anticipates particularly strong demand for models handling routine transactions with company-specific details. A corporation's own model may retain institutional knowledge as general counsel come and go. These are buyer-side departments, distinct from law firms and software providers.

Legal-AI and research vendors: LexisNexis, Westlaw and Harvey have incentives to develop specialized capabilities and trusted security arrangements. Vendors may benefit from serving many firms, while open-source alternatives and consolidated firms' in-house development or volume bargaining can threaten their positions.

Clients and the public: Clients may receive cheaper, faster services and become more attached to a firm's model than to an individual lawyer. Fagan also expects occasional nonlawyer users to benefit from high-quality open-source models. The paper does not quantify a reduction in unmet civil legal need. People affected by changes to rights and resource allocation remain beneficiaries of human advocacy and empathy in his account.

Judges, legislators and other lawmakers: Models can assist routine adjudication and offer information or policy options, but Fagan expects humans to retain control over precedent, social goals and rights allocation. Transactional, copyright, compliance and tort practitioners initially gain new work as AI-related questions emerge; this demand may recede as those questions become routine.
